lesson.title: Weighing Your Way to an Answer: Gravimetric Analysis
lesson.summary: Gravimetric analysis determines how much of a substance is present in a sample by converting the substance of interest into an insoluble precipitate, then carefully isolating, drying, and weighing that precipitate to work backward to the original amount.
lesson.body:
Gravimetric analysis is one of the oldest and most reliable quantitative techniques in chemistry, and it rests on a simple idea: if you can convert an unknown amount of some ion into a solid that is completely insoluble, and you can collect every last bit of that solid without losing any, then a single mass measurement on a balance is enough to work backward, through stoichiometry, to the amount of that ion in the original sample. It draws directly on precipitation reactions to choose a reagent that will pull the target ion out of solution as a solid, and it draws on ordinary stoichiometry to convert the mass of that solid into the mass of whatever was being measured in the first place.

The general procedure runs as follows. A sample of known mass is dissolved in water. A precipitating reagent is added in excess, well beyond what is needed stoichiometrically, to make sure the target ion is removed from solution as completely as possible. The resulting precipitate is filtered out, washed to remove any impurities clinging to it, and dried, often by heating, until repeated weighings show the mass has stopped changing, confirming all the water is gone. Only then is the precipitate weighed on an analytical balance.

Here is a worked example. A 0.5000 g sample of an unknown chloride salt is dissolved in water, and an excess of silver nitrate is added, precipitating all the chloride ion as AgCl according to Ag+ + Cl- -> AgCl(s). After filtering, washing, and drying, the solid AgCl is weighed and found to have a mass of 0.3220 g. To find the percent chloride by mass in the original sample, first convert the AgCl mass to moles using its molar mass, 107.87 g/mol for silver plus 35.45 g/mol for chlorine, or 143.32 g/mol: 0.3220 g divided by 143.32 g/mol equals 0.002247 mol AgCl. Since each mole of AgCl contains exactly one mole of chlorine, there are also 0.002247 mol of Cl. Converting that to mass using chlorine's molar mass of 35.45 g/mol gives 0.002247 mol times 35.45 g/mol, which equals 0.07966 g of Cl. Finally, divide by the original sample mass and multiply by 100 percent: 0.07966 g divided by 0.5000 g equals 0.1593, or 15.9 percent chloride by mass.

The accuracy of gravimetric analysis depends entirely on two things going right: the precipitate has to be genuinely insoluble enough that essentially none of the target ion is left behind in solution, and the isolation process, filtering, washing, and drying, has to lose essentially none of the solid that did form. Because it needs no specialized instrument beyond a balance and standard glassware, gravimetric analysis remains a dependable, if slow, way to determine composition with high precision, and it is often used to check or calibrate faster instrumental methods.
